issue_context.title: Remove PodBackoffMap
issue_context.body:
The PodBackoffMap (pkg/scheduler/internal/queue) is used to calculate backoff for pods.
This structure is cleaned up periodically, losing backoff information. We added a mitigation #87616 which is being backported down to 1.15
However, there are still cases were a backoff for a pod will be lost (such as when a cluster doesn't change much). But, as noted in the PR discussion, we don't need the Map anymore, as the information is stored in PodInfo. We just need the helper method that calculates the backoff from the last schedule attempt and number of retries.

#78849 was going in this direction, but it is now stalled.

/sig scheduling
/good-first-issue
comments:
yes, the PodBackoff struct would just have global configuration. It doesn't need any other information. Everything should accept `PodInfo`, instead of `v1.Pod`. `PodInfo` has the last attempt timestamp and number of attempts.

At the end of the day, every pod that doesn't get scheduled will be "backing off", just with different timeouts.

> after this change, movePodsToActiveOrBackoffQueue actually move all pods to backoff queue.

Not true, because the timeout might have passed already :)
Thanks @alculquicondor for the confirmation. I have sent a PR.

review_comments:
maybe we can have another operation that does a clock Step?
I'm actually not sure what we are trying to test here.
there is an existing operation: moveClockForward
shouldn't we use a fake clock here too? Otherwise, how are we guaranteeing that this test is not flaky?
yes we need, done.
Add unit test for `Update` that exercises what we discussed.

(not quite related the deleted lines)

In the update case, should we reset the backoff expiry? If yes, the current logic doesn't work as in `updatePod()`, it actually just copy newPod (*v1.Pod) to oldPodInfo and return. In other words, oldPodInfo.attempts are kept and hence be honored when calculating the backoff timeout.

cc @alculquicondor
To preserve the current behavior, we would reset Attempts to zero. And we should document this in the comment of `Update`. Agreed?

It's the tricky part. On one hand, to preserve the "Update" semantics, we should look at it as a "new" pod, hence reset its backoff timer. However, on the other hand, to achieve that, it seems the only way is to reset `podInfo.Attempts`, and that sort of breaks the semantics of "attempts" - in a metrics point of view, "attempts" records the number of a Pod's lifespan scheduling attempts :)

> An alternative would be to reset Timestamp with the next backoff timeout. That way, it immediately goes to activeQ, but if would preserve its backoff.

Are you referring to changing the semantics of `podInfo.TimeStamp`? If so, I don't think it's necessary.

Basically, the key point I want to raise is:

- With this PR, for every case (update or whatever others), an existing Pod's backoff is kept
- In the before, e.g., for the Update case, as we called `clearPodBackoff`, the updated pod was (1) put back into activeQ, and (2) its backoff timer was reset.

So we should discuss the scenarios of resetting backoff timer here, whether we should, or shouldn't, e.g., for the Update case.

A couple of things:
1) It seems that we are preserving the semantics of the backoff start time (```podInfo.Timestamp``` is updated when ```podLastUpdateTime``` used to be updated), this is good...

2) Number of ```podInfo.Attempts``` doesn't have the same semantics as ```podAttempts``` map, the latter gets reset on update, the former doesn't.

Two options:
1)  We add ```backoffAttempts``` to podInfo to maintain the current semantics . 
2) On update, the pod is placed in the activeQ directly (line 478 below), so it is getting an immediate chance for reevaluation. So, maybe it is not so bad if we assume that the pod should not have its attempts reset to 0 when calculating the next backoff if the pod didn't get scheduled.

option 2 means no changes from what this PR is already doing, right?

I would say this is reasonable. But we just need to unit test this.

> So, maybe it is not so bad if we assume that the pod should not have its attempts reset to 0 when calculating the next backoff if the pod didn't get scheduled.

It's exactly the point I want to get into a consensus. I'm fine with this option.
I think this is reasonable.
@notpad was there a unit test for this? If not, please add one.
Great to see this going away.

Let's not change the output.
We could have some pods with different timestamps so that some would be in active and some in backoffq.
use Step here too.

previously the unschedule pods will be moved to activeQ if it doesn't exists in PodBackoffMap.
Now we should wait for backoff to complete or move the clock

A few things:

- This test is titled: `MoveAllToActiveQueue`, which is probably just outdated.
- Why aren't pods being moved back to active? Don't they have 0 attempts? Do we care about 0?
- I suggest we grab the fake clock, set some timestamps and attempts in the pod infos, and make this test case more interesting. But... isn't this already covered in `TestPendingPodsMetric`?

> Why aren't pods being moved back to active? Don't they have 0 attempts? Do we care about 0?

0 attempts means podInitialBackoffDuration

Originally, isPodBackingoff checked two things: pod exist in the PodBackoffMap and the backoff time is after ```clock.Now()```.  This unit test didn't properly add the pod to the unschedulable queue: it directly placed the pod in the queue instead of calling AddUnschedulableIfNotPresent, which means the pod didn't exist in PodBackoffMap, and so isPodBackingoff returned false and MoveAllToActiveOrBackoffQueue placed the pod in the active queue directly.

Now that we are basing isPodBackingoff only on backoff time, it return true, and so MoveAllToActiveOrBackoffQueue is placing the pods in the backoffQ.

To avoid confusion, we should remove the `addOrUpdateUnschedulabePod` function. Also, it's worth noting that `AddUnschedulableIfNotPresent` doesn't increase the Attempts counter either. This is managed by the core scheduler itself.
